text: Phone only charges with the original charger. A different charger (same phone brand claim, different amperage) shows 'charging' briefly then stops, or doesn't charge at all.

metadata.correct_diagnosis: Charger/cable mismatch — the alternate charger doesn't meet the current/voltage handshake the phone's charging IC expects, often due to a non-original or underpowered charger, not a hardware fault in the phone.
diagnostic_steps: Test with 2-3 different known-good cables/chargers, not just one alternate.
Check if charging works via a USB port on a laptop (lower current) — if it charges slowly there, port and battery are likely fine.
Inspect the charging port visually/with a flashlight for debris before assuming electrical fault.
metadata.fix_summary: No repair needed if isolated to charger — advise customer on compatible charger; only proceed to port/IC-level diagnosis if original charger also fails intermittently.
metadata.generated_question_example: A customer says their phone charges fine with the box charger but not with a friend's charger. Do you replace the charging port immediately? Why or why not?

text: Phone doesn't charge at all with any charger. No response, no charging icon, screen stays off when plugged in.

metadata.correct_diagnosis: Debris (lint, dust, oxidation) lodged in the charging port blocking pin contact — extremely common and often mistaken for a bigger hardware fault.
distractor_causes: Battery is completely dead and needs replacement
diagnostic_steps: Visually inspect the port with a flashlight and magnification before opening the device.
Gently clean with a wooden toothpick or anti-static brush, no metal objects.
Retest with original charger after cleaning before assuming battery or board failure.
metadata.fix_summary: Clean the port; retest. Only escalate to battery/board diagnostics if cleaning doesn't resolve it.
metadata.generated_question_example: Before you conclude a phone's motherboard is dead because it won't charge, what's the first thing you should physically check, and why?

text: After a previous repair (screen + battery both replaced elsewhere), phone now charges very slowly and overheats near the charging port, but only when the screen is on and in use.

metadata.device_context: Infinix Note-class phone, recently had screen AND battery replaced by another technician
metadata.correct_diagnosis: Overheating tied specifically to screen-on usage suggests a possible short or poor connection from the screen replacement (e.g. a pinched flex cable near the board), drawing excess current — not the battery itself, even though a battery was also recently replaced and is an easy scapegoat.
distractor_causes: Charging port was damaged during the previous repair
diagnostic_steps: Isolate variables: does overheating happen with screen off but phone actively charging? If not, focus on the display assembly/flex routing, not the battery.
Reopen the device and inspect flex cable routing near the previous screen replacement for pinching or improper seating.
Only replace the battery again if a load test shows it's degrading independently of the screen-on condition.
metadata.fix_summary: Re-seat/re-route the display flex cable; avoid assuming the most recently replaced part (battery) is automatically at fault just because it's newest.
metadata.generated_question_example: A phone had its screen and battery both replaced elsewhere last week. Now it overheats while charging, but only when the screen is actively on. Which part would you investigate first, and why not the battery?

text: Phone shows 100% battery, then suddenly shuts off within minutes of unplugging, even though it was 'fully charged'.

metadata.correct_diagnosis: Swollen or degraded battery cell — the battery reports voltage that appears high but can't sustain load, a classic sign of internal cell degradation rather than a reporting/software issue alone.
diagnostic_steps: Physically inspect the battery for swelling (screen lifting slightly at edges is a common tell) before assuming it's purely software.
Load-test: check voltage drop under active use (camera, screen brightness) vs idle.
If swelling is present, treat as urgent — safety risk, not just a performance issue.
metadata.fix_summary: Replace battery. Flag swollen batteries as a safety issue requiring careful disposal, not just a routine swap.
metadata.generated_question_example: A phone shows full battery then shuts off almost immediately after unplugging. What physical check should you do before assuming this is a software calibration issue?

text: Screen shows a dark patch that slowly spreads over days, like ink spreading under the glass, though the phone still functions and responds to touch.

metadata.correct_diagnosis: Liquid damage to the LCD layer — the spreading dark patch pattern strongly suggests moisture intrusion degrading the display over time, not a static defect or software issue.
diagnostic_steps: Ask the customer about any recent water/liquid exposure, even minor (rain, spill, humidity).
Check for corrosion on the display connector when opening the device.
Distinguish from dead pixels: dead pixels are static and don't spread; this pattern growing over days points to ongoing liquid damage.
metadata.fix_summary: Replace the LCD/display assembly; also check and clean the board for corrosion if liquid damage is confirmed.
metadata.generated_question_example: A customer's screen has a dark patch that has grown bigger every day for a week. Is this the same issue as a few dead pixels? What would you ask the customer?

text: Touch is unresponsive only in one corner of the screen, rest of the screen works fine.

metadata.device_context: Generic Android phone with a screen protector installed
metadata.correct_diagnosis: Localized touch failure is more consistent with a partial digitizer fault or a lifted/loose flex connector at that specific edge, or even a bubbled/damaged screen protector interfering — not necessarily a full digitizer or board-level failure.
diagnostic_steps: First remove the screen protector entirely and retest — cheap or damaged protectors can cause localized touch issues.
If issue persists, check if the affected corner correlates with where the display flex connects to the board (common failure zone).
Only conclude full digitizer replacement is needed after ruling out the protector and connector reseating.
metadata.fix_summary: Remove protector and retest first; if unresolved, reseat or replace the display flex connection before replacing the whole screen.
metadata.generated_question_example: Only one corner of a phone's screen isn't responding to touch. What's the cheapest, fastest thing to check before you quote the customer for a full screen replacement?

text: Speaker sound is muffled and quiet, especially during calls, but loud enough during music playback through the same speaker.

metadata.correct_diagnosis: Dust/debris accumulation in the speaker mesh/grill is a very common and cheap-to-fix cause of muffled sound, distinct from actual speaker hardware failure — the fact that music playback is louder than calls can indicate the earpiece speaker (used in calls) vs the loudspeaker (used for media) are different components, worth distinguishing.
distractor_causes: Speaker component is fully damaged and must be replaced
diagnostic_steps: Clarify with the customer: is this the earpiece speaker (calls, held to ear) or the loudspeaker (media, speakerphone) that's affected — they're usually separate components.
Clean the relevant speaker grill with a soft dry brush before assuming hardware failure.
Retest with a diagnostic dialer code or app to isolate speaker component tests, if available.
metadata.fix_summary: Clean grill first; if still muffled after cleaning, then test/replace the specific speaker component (earpiece vs loudspeaker) identified.
metadata.generated_question_example: A customer says calls sound muffled but music is fine. Are these likely the same speaker component? What would you clean or test first before quoting a speaker replacement?

text: Caller can't hear the phone's user during calls, but voice recording (voice memo app) works fine.

metadata.correct_diagnosis: Since the voice memo app works, the microphone hardware itself is functional — the issue is more likely in call-specific audio routing/software or a call-only microphone path (some phones have a secondary mic dedicated to calls/noise cancellation) rather than the primary mic being dead.
diagnostic_steps: Confirm the distinction: does voice recording via an app work? If yes, don't jump to 'mic hardware needs replacement.'
Check if this phone has multiple microphones (common on mid/high-end phones for noise cancellation) — a secondary mic fault can affect calls specifically.
Test with a different calling app (WhatsApp vs native dialer) to rule out software/app-specific bugs before hardware.
metadata.fix_summary: Don't replace the primary mic if recording works; investigate secondary mic or software call routing first.
metadata.generated_question_example: A phone's voice memo recordings sound fine, but callers can't hear the user on phone calls. Does this mean the microphone is faulty? What should you check first?

text: Phone turns off randomly during use, no pattern to when, sometimes works fine for hours, sometimes shuts off within minutes. Charges normally when off.

metadata.correct_diagnosis: Random unpredictable shutdowns with normal charging behavior often point to a loose/poor board-level connection (e.g. battery connector, power IC solder joint) or a software crash loop, rather than a straightforward battery failure — battery issues are usually more predictable and load-correlated, not fully random.
distractor_causes: Battery needs replacement (most common first guess)
diagnostic_steps: Ask about correlation: does it happen more during heavy use (gaming, camera) suggesting heat/power draw, or truly randomly including at idle?
Reseat the battery connector on the board as a first low-cost step.
If random even at idle with low load, consider software crash logs (if accessible) before assuming hardware.
metadata.fix_summary: Reseat connections first; escalate to board-level diagnosis only if reseating doesn't resolve it, and don't default to battery replacement without ruling out connector/software causes.
metadata.generated_question_example: A phone shuts off randomly with no clear pattern, but charges fine. A junior tech wants to replace the battery immediately. What would you check first, and why might random (not load-correlated) shutdowns not be a simple battery issue?

text: Phone shows the brand logo, restarts, shows logo again, in a continuous loop. Doesn't reach the home screen.

metadata.device_context: Generic Android phone stuck in boot loop after a failed OS update
metadata.correct_diagnosis: A boot loop immediately following a failed/interrupted OS update is a strong signal of corrupted firmware/software, not hardware failure — this is the classic case for reflashing rather than component replacement.
distractor_causes: Hardware failure (board or storage chip is dead)
diagnostic_steps: Confirm timeline with customer: did this start right after an update or app install? Strong software signal if yes.
Attempt boot into recovery/download mode — if the phone responds to button combinations for recovery mode, the hardware/board is very likely fine.
Only suspect hardware if the phone doesn't respond to recovery mode attempts at all.
metadata.fix_summary: Reflash firmware via recovery/download mode tools appropriate to the device; back up data first if at all possible before wiping.
metadata.generated_question_example: A phone is stuck looping on the boot logo right after a failed software update. Should you open the phone to check hardware first, or try something else? What's your first diagnostic step?

text: Customer forgot their screen lock PIN and wants it removed/bypassed.

metadata.correct_diagnosis: This is a passcode/lock removal request, not a hardware fault. Ethically and often legally, technicians should verify proof of ownership before bypassing any lock screen, to avoid facilitating theft of stolen devices.
diagnostic_steps: Request proof of ownership (receipt, ID matching device registration, or account recovery info) before attempting bypass.
Distinguish between owner-forgotten-PIN cases (legitimate) vs unclear-ownership cases (red flag).
Use manufacturer-supported account recovery methods where possible instead of third-party bypass tools that may violate device security intentionally.
metadata.fix_summary: Verify ownership first; use legitimate recovery methods over generic bypass tools where possible.
metadata.generated_question_example: A customer brings in a phone locked with a PIN they say they forgot and asks you to unlock it. What should you check before doing anything technical?

text: After a factory reset, phone asks for the previous Google account login (Factory Reset Protection) and the customer doesn't remember the account credentials.

metadata.device_context: Generic Android phone, previously factory reset
metadata.correct_diagnosis: FRP triggers specifically because the device was reset without first removing the Google account — this is expected security behavior, not a fault. Same ownership-verification caution as lock bypass applies, since FRP removal tools are also commonly misused on stolen devices.
diagnostic_steps: Verify ownership (proof of purchase, matching ID) before attempting any FRP bypass.
Try legitimate account recovery via Google's own recovery flow first (if the customer has any residual account access, e.g. recovery email/phone).
Only use bypass tools as a last resort, and be aware some methods can trip additional security flags on certain brands.
metadata.fix_summary: Prioritize legitimate account recovery over bypass tools; verify ownership regardless of method used.
metadata.generated_question_example: A customer's phone is locked by Factory Reset Protection after a reset and they don't remember their Google login. What's the responsible first step before using any bypass tool?

text: Phone charges fine when the screen is off, but stops charging (or charges very slowly) whenever the screen is on and being used.

metadata.correct_diagnosis: This pattern usually means power draw while screen-on exceeds what the charger/port can supply on top of active usage — often normal behavior with a low-wattage charger or cable on a phone with a bright/large screen, not necessarily a fault at all.
diagnostic_steps: Check the charger's wattage rating against the phone's expected fast-charge spec — a mismatch is the most likely and cheapest-to-rule-out explanation.
Test with a known higher-wattage original-spec charger before assuming any component fault.
Only investigate port/battery hardware if the issue persists even with a confirmed correctly-rated charger.
metadata.fix_summary: Often no repair needed — educate the customer on charger wattage; escalate to hardware diagnosis only if a proper charger still shows the issue.
metadata.generated_question_example: A phone won't charge while the screen is on and in use, but charges fine with the screen off. Is this necessarily a broken charging port? What would you check first?

text: After a screen replacement, display looks fine but touch is unresponsive across the whole screen.

metadata.device_context: Generic Android phone after a screen replacement done elsewhere
metadata.correct_diagnosis: Full touch failure right after a screen replacement is very often a loose or improperly seated digitizer/display flex connector from the installation itself, not necessarily a defective replacement part — this should be checked before assuming the part is bad.
distractor_causes: The new replacement screen is defective and must be swapped again immediately
diagnostic_steps: Reopen and check that all display flex connectors are fully and correctly seated, especially the touch-specific connector if separate from the display connector.
Check for any pinched or damaged flex cables from the reassembly process.
Only conclude the replacement part is defective after confirming correct, undamaged connector seating.
metadata.fix_summary: Reseat/inspect connectors first; avoid unnecessarily swapping the part again if it's a seating issue.
metadata.generated_question_example: A screen was just replaced and the display looks perfect, but touch doesn't work at all. Should your first assumption be that the new screen is defective? What would you check before reordering a part?

text: Phone's back cover appears slightly puffed/lifted at the edges; phone still turns on and functions.

metadata.device_context: Generic Android phone, several years old
metadata.correct_diagnosis: A puffed back cover on an aging phone is a classic external sign of a swollen battery — this should be treated as a safety priority (fire/chemical risk), not a cosmetic issue, even though the phone still functions normally.
diagnostic_steps: Do not press on the puffed area or attempt to force the back cover flat.
Advise the customer to stop using/charging the phone until the battery is inspected/replaced.
Handle and dispose of the swollen battery according to safe battery-handling practice, not as ordinary e-waste.
metadata.fix_summary: Treat as urgent safety issue; replace the battery promptly and handle disposal carefully.
metadata.generated_question_example: A customer says their phone's back cover looks puffed but the phone still works fine, so they're not worried about it. How would you explain the urgency of this to them?

text: Charging cable feels loose in the port and phone only charges when the cable is held at a specific angle.

metadata.correct_diagnosis: Worn or bent charging port pins causing intermittent physical contact — a mechanical port issue, not battery or software.
diagnostic_steps: Physically wiggle-test the cable at different angles while observing the charging indicator.
Inspect port pins visually for bending or wear compared to a known-good port.
Rule out cable-side wear by testing the same cable in another device.
metadata.fix_summary: Replace the charging port assembly if pins are confirmed bent/worn.
metadata.generated_question_example: A phone only charges when the cable is held at a certain angle. Is this more likely a battery, software, or mechanical issue? Why?

text: Battery percentage jumps erratically — e.g. 40% suddenly shows 15%, then back to 35% seconds later.

metadata.correct_diagnosis: Battery cell degradation causing unstable voltage readings, which the phone's battery gauge misreports as erratic percentage jumps — a battery health issue, not a display or port fault.
distractor_causes: Screen display glitch unrelated to battery
diagnostic_steps: Confirm the jumps happen regardless of charging state (plugged in or not).
Check battery health via diagnostic dialer codes or a battery health app if available.
Rule out display issues by cross-checking percentage in two different places (status bar vs settings).
metadata.fix_summary: Replace battery; erratic percentage reporting with a healthy battery would be rare and points to software, but should be checked after hardware is ruled out.
metadata.generated_question_example: A phone's battery percentage jumps around unpredictably even while just sitting idle. What would you check to confirm this is the battery and not the screen or software?

text: Screen displays fine but has a few thin vertical lines of discoloration that appeared right after a drop.

metadata.correct_diagnosis: Impact damage to the LCD's internal ribbon/connector from the drop, causing physical display artifacts — directly tied to the drop, not software or a coincidental defect.
distractor_causes: Pre-existing manufacturing defect unrelated to the drop
diagnostic_steps: Correlate timing precisely: did the lines appear immediately after the drop or gradually before it?
Rule out software by booting into recovery mode — if lines persist outside the OS, it's hardware.
Check if lines shift or change when gently flexing the screen edge (indicates loose connector vs panel damage).
metadata.fix_summary: Replace the LCD/display assembly; if lines shift with flexing, try reseating the connector first before replacing.
metadata.generated_question_example: A customer's screen shows thin colored lines that appeared right after they dropped the phone. How would you confirm this is drop-related hardware damage and not a coincidence?

text: Touch becomes unresponsive or erratic specifically in humid weather or when the user's hands are wet.

metadata.device_context: Generic Android phone, user has wet/sweaty hands often
metadata.correct_diagnosis: Capacitive touchscreens are sensitive to moisture on the screen surface or fingers — this is often expected behavior with wet hands, not a hardware fault, unless it happens even with fully dry hands and screen.
diagnostic_steps: Test touch response with the screen and hands completely dry before assuming any fault.
Ask the customer to describe exactly when it happens — only in rain/humidity, or also indoors when dry.
If it only occurs with visible moisture present, this may not need repair at all.
metadata.fix_summary: Often no repair needed; educate customer on capacitive touchscreen behavior with moisture. Investigate hardware only if issue persists when fully dry.
metadata.generated_question_example: A customer complains their touchscreen doesn't work well in the rain or with wet hands. Is this necessarily a hardware fault? What would you ask before quoting a digitizer replacement?

text: Speaker produces a crackling/distorted sound only at high volume; sounds fine at low-medium volume.

metadata.correct_diagnosis: Distortion specifically at high volume, with clean sound at lower volume, often indicates a partially damaged speaker cone or a loose speaker housing rattling — not full speaker failure, and sometimes fixable without full replacement.
distractor_causes: Speaker is completely dead and must be replaced
diagnostic_steps: Test across the full volume range to confirm the distortion threshold precisely.
Check if the speaker housing/frame is loose or if the rattling is from a loose back cover instead of the speaker itself.
Try reseating the speaker component before ordering a replacement part.
metadata.fix_summary: Reseat speaker/check housing first; replace only if distortion persists after confirming secure mounting.
metadata.generated_question_example: A phone's speaker crackles at high volume but sounds clean otherwise. Does this always mean the speaker is dead? What else could cause this?

text: Caller says the user's voice sounds muffled/far away during calls.

metadata.device_context: Generic Android phone with a case/cover installed
metadata.correct_diagnosis: A phone case or screen protector covering or partially blocking the microphone hole is a very common and easily overlooked cause of muffled call audio.
diagnostic_steps: Remove any case/cover and retest a call before any internal diagnosis.
Visually check the mic hole for blockage from the case design itself, not just debris.
If muffled audio persists with the case removed, proceed to check for physical debris or hardware fault.
metadata.fix_summary: Often no repair needed — remove obstructing case; investigate mic hardware only if issue persists without any case.
metadata.generated_question_example: A customer says people can't hear them clearly on calls. What's a completely non-technical first check before opening the phone?

text: Phone only shuts off unexpectedly when the battery is below roughly 20-30%, never at higher charge levels.

metadata.correct_diagnosis: A battery that can't sustain voltage under load as charge drops is a classic aging-battery symptom — the phone's voltage cutoff is being triggered prematurely because the battery can't maintain sufficient voltage at lower charge percentages, even though it reports a non-zero percentage.
diagnostic_steps: Confirm the pattern precisely: does it always happen below a similar percentage threshold, or truly randomly?
If threshold-correlated, this points strongly to battery capacity/voltage sag rather than software or button issues.
Load-test the battery (e.g. camera flash use) at that charge level to see if voltage drops sharply.
metadata.fix_summary: Replace the battery; threshold-correlated shutdowns are a strong, specific signal distinct from the fully random shutdown case covered elsewhere.
metadata.generated_question_example: A phone always shuts off once it drops below about 25% battery, never above that. Is this the same kind of problem as a phone shutting off completely at random? What does the pattern tell you?

text: After a factory reset done by the customer themselves (not a failed update), phone runs noticeably slower and apps crash more than before.

metadata.correct_diagnosis: Post-reset slowness with crashing is more often caused by a bad/corrupted restore of backed-up apps and data, or a pre-existing storage near-full condition carried over, rather than new hardware failure coinciding suspiciously with the reset.
diagnostic_steps: Check available storage space — a reset doesn't help if the backup restore fills storage back up near capacity.
Ask if the slowness started immediately after restoring apps from backup vs immediately after the reset itself.
Run a storage health check only after ruling out software/restore causes, since hardware failure coinciding exactly with a user-initiated reset is less likely.
metadata.fix_summary: Investigate restored data/storage fullness before assuming new hardware failure; clean reinstall without full backup restore as a test.
metadata.generated_question_example: A customer resets their own phone to fix slowness, restores their backup, and it's still slow. Should you suspect new hardware failure, or something else first?

text: Phone charges normally but customer reports it now takes noticeably longer to charge than before a previous charging port repair.

metadata.device_context: Generic Android phone, previously repaired for charging port by another technician
metadata.correct_diagnosis: A previous charging port repair using a non-original or lower-spec port component can silently disable fast-charging support even though basic charging works — worth checking before assuming battery degradation.
distractor_causes: Battery has degraded coincidentally around the same time
diagnostic_steps: Ask what charger/cable is being used and whether it's the same one used before the repair.
Check if the phone's fast-charge indicator/icon still appears when charging (many phones show this).
Compare charging speed with a different, confirmed-original-spec port/cable combination if possible before concluding it's the battery.
metadata.fix_summary: If fast-charge capability was lost, the replacement port component is likely non-original spec; consider a proper fast-charge-compatible port replacement rather than assuming battery fault.
metadata.generated_question_example: A phone charges slower than before, after having its charging port replaced elsewhere a month ago. What would you check before quoting a battery replacement?

text: Customer says they bought the phone secondhand and it's locked with someone else's PIN/account, and they have no proof of purchase.

metadata.correct_diagnosis: This scenario carries a real risk the device may be stolen or improperly resold while still tied to the original owner — this is fundamentally different from the earlier 'forgot own PIN' case and should be handled with more caution, not treated as a routine unlock job.
diagnostic_steps: Distinguish this clearly from a simple forgotten-PIN case: no proof of purchase plus secondhand origin is a higher-risk combination.
Ask for any documentation of the secondhand sale (receipt, messages with seller, IMEI check against loss/theft databases if accessible).
Consider declining the bypass request if ownership can't be reasonably established, even if the customer seems genuine.
metadata.fix_summary: Treat with more scrutiny than a standard forgotten-PIN job; document your reasoning if you proceed or decline.
metadata.generated_question_example: A customer wants a secondhand phone unlocked but has no proof of purchase and doesn't know the previous owner. How is this different from someone forgetting their own phone's PIN, and how should you handle it?
